title: Augustine of Canterbury
hookLine: sent from Rome to England, he's told: don't destroy their temples, bless them

lines: ON THE ROAD, THEY LOSE THEIR NERVE.
ASK THE POPE TO CALL IT OFF.
cards: On the road, they lose their nerve. A group of monks has left Rome on Gregory's orders, headed for the far island of the English.

Bede, who tells the story, says fear seized them: a fierce, unbelieving people, a language none of them could speak. So they stop, and send their leader back to ask the pope to call the whole thing off.
Their leader is a monk named Augustine. Not the Augustine of the Confessions; another Augustine.
Gregory sends him back with a letter that says, more or less, keep going: better not to start a good work than to turn back from it. So they go on.

teach.h: A CROSS AND A PAINTED PICTURE.
teach.b: They land in Kent, and the king, Ethelbert, comes to meet them. Bede says he insisted on the open air, in case they tried some kind of magic indoors.
The monks walk up carrying a silver cross and a picture of Christ painted on a board, singing as they come. The king's answer is careful and fair.

teach.h: YOUR WORDS ARE NEW TO ME.
teach.b: Your words are good, he says, but they're new to me, and I can't just leave what my people have always held. But you've come a long way. Stay.
We'll feed you, and you can speak to anyone who will listen. Later, Gregory writes a letter about what to do with the old temples of the English. Bede keeps it.
Gregory says he has thought about it for a long time.

Don't tear the temples down. Take out the idols, bless the buildings with water, set up altars, and let them become places of worship to God, so people can keep coming to the places they already know.
Even their old feast days should become feasts of thanksgiving.

teach.h: STEP BY STEP, NOT IN LEAPS.
teach.b: Then a sentence about how people change: whoever wants to climb a high place goes up step by step, not in leaps. Two cautions.

Bede also keeps an earlier letter in which Gregory urged the king to overthrow the shrines, so this was a change of mind, not his only word. And it was still a mission: the old gods' images were removed.
But in the later letter Gregory chose to keep what he could: the buildings, the gathering places, the habit of feasting together.

how: Anglican and Catholic Christians remember Augustine of Canterbury as the monk sent by Gregory to Kent, and the archbishop of Canterbury's chair is traditionally called the chair of Saint Augustine.

games.q: you're one of the monks on the road from Rome. you're afraid of the people ahead and you don't speak their language. what do you do?
o: stop, and send your leader back to ask the pope to cancel.
games.why: they stopped and sent Augustine back to Gregory. Gregory sent him back with a letter: better not to start a good work than to turn back from it.

practice: Picture a place you've been trying to change: a team at work, a family habit, a neighborhood.

Before you think about what's wrong with it, find one thing that's already good there, a gathering, a tradition, a person who keeps it going, and see it clearly. If you pray, give thanks for it; if not, just name it to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Augustine. The monk who nearly turned back, reached Kent, and carried Gregory's advice: keep the old places, and bless them.

carryVoice: Your line: bless, don't destroy. Not in leaps, but step by step. Day seven hundred ninety, done.
